intro: Emma Eames recorded Beach’s Browning song for Victor on 18 May 1908, a remake of her 1905 recording. She sings the whole song, including both of Beach’s settings of the opening lines, in under a minute.

sections.mNote: The same lines restart, piano and a tempo.

sections.label: B · Crescendo, then “God’s in his heaven”

cues.title: Victor 88008, 18 May 1908
cues.text: Eames recorded the song with piano in New York on 18 May 1908. Victor issued it on a single-sided 12-inch disc, number 88008, where it followed Henschel’s Spring. The May 1908 catalogue lists the same number for her 1905 recording, coupled with Hahn’s L’Incrédule.
cues.evidence: The Discography of American Historical Recordings lists matrix C-6203, take 1, 18 May 1908, New York, on Victor 88008, with the note “Also recorded as C-2314” (https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/200007142). The July 1909 Victor catalogue, p. 55, gives Spring and The Year’s at the Spring for 88008 (https://archive.org/details/newvictorrecordc00vict). The May 1908 catalogue, p. 45, lists 88008 as L’Incrédule and The Year’s at the Spring (https://archive.org/details/newvictorrecordc00vict_0); the Discography lists matrix C-2314, the 1905 recording, under 88008 as well (https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/55891).

cues.title: Held note on “right”
cues.text: After ff on “All’s”, the voice holds “right” for more than two bars over repeated piano chords. A ritenuto leads to “world”, held a tempo for more than two bars, and the piano ends the song on a fermata chord.
cues.evidence: The 1900 edition, p. 5 (B♭ edition): ff at “All’s”, then “right” tied across two bars and an eighth over repeated chords marked marcato, “rit.” in the 4/4 bar, “a tempo” at “world!”, held over two bars, and a fermata on the closing bar (https://archive.org/details/per_women-composers-collection_the-years-at-the-spring_1900).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Discography of American Historical Recordings describes the matrix as “Soprano vocal solo, with piano” and names no pianist; the Romophone booklet lists this track among those with piano and gives no accompanist.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Beach’s Browning setting, complete: both settings of the opening lines, then the rest of the poem. It is the second of two songs on one 12-inch Victor side, after George Henschel’s “Spring”. The key is D♭ major.
fields.note: The pairing with Henschel’s “Spring” is documented by the Discography of American Historical Recordings and the July 1909 catalogue, and the Romophone track list gives “Spring” and “The Year’s at the Spring” as parts of one matrix. That the track is the whole song is inferred by comparing its sung pitches with the vocal part of the 1900 edition (B♭ version, read in D♭): the leaps to E♭, F and G♭ of the first setting fall in the first eleven seconds, and the restart on p. 4 follows at about fifteen seconds. No source states it. The key is inferred from the closing chord and from the key printed on the label of Eames’s 1905 recording of the song. The edition she sang from (the 1900 print offers B♭ and D♭ versions) has not been seen.

fields.label: Recorded

fields.note: The July 1909 catalogue lists the disc on the Emma Eames page at $3.00.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The same number had carried Eames’s 1905 recording of the song with Hahn’s “L’Incrédule” (listed in the May 1908 catalogue); the July 1909 catalogue lists the 1908 pairing under it. The Discography of American Historical Recordings also lists IRCC-194 and AGSB-22 reissues of this matrix.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Both songs are on one matrix, which the Discography of American Historical Recordings titles “Spring” with “Year’s at the spring” as an additional title, and which it notes was “Also recorded as C-2314”, the 1905 recording. The Romophone booklet gives C 6203-1.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Ward Marston, transfers and audio restoration; Ward Marston, producer; Virginia Barder, executive producer. Romophone 81001-2, CD 2, track 13.
fields.note: These credits are printed for the whole set. The Internet Archive item (whose own text gives the set number as 81000-2) names the set and the track but no separate engineer for the file; the person who ripped and uploaded it is not credited as an engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive descriptions date the set to 1993; a Beach discography gives 1995, and the booklet scan prints no year. The dates of the disc transfer and the restoration are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 8 April 2025 is a copying event, not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Restoration by Ward Marston for the Romophone CD, with no settings stated; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV or FLAC rip of the CD.
fields.note: The closing chord of this track is D♭ major at concert pitch, within about a tenth of a semitone of A = 440 Hz. Two other Internet Archive transfers of the same disc (item 78_springbyearofthespring_146_06, the second labelled IRCC 194-A) play about three per cent faster, half a semitone sharp of this file. Stylus, equalisation and noise reduction are not documented. About five seconds of silence follow the last chord.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Out of copyright: Beach died in 1944 and Browning in 1889.
fields.note: Life-plus-70 terms have run out for both; the first edition was published in the United States in 1900. This covers the song, not modern editions.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: first published by July 1909 on Victor 88008 (recorded 18 May 1908). The Archive item carries the Public Domain Mark.
fields.note: Selected under the project’s us-published-before-cutoff rule: a recording first published before 1923 had exhausted its federal term by 31 December 2021. The July 1909 catalogue is the dated source for 1909 as the latest year of first publication. The audio is the Romophone restoration by Ward Marston. The Public Domain Mark was applied by the uploader, is a statement by the person who identified the work, and is not the basis for publication. The scanned booklet carries no copyright notice for the transfers (its only © line is for the essay; the tray insert is not in the scan), and the track is one continuous performance in score order. The Ninth Circuit held in ABS Entertainment v. CBS (2018) that a remaster distinguished only by change of medium, declicking or noise reduction generally lacks the originality needed for a new copyright. No source consulted shows Romophone or Marston dedicating the restoration to the public domain, and a claim outside the United States has not been ruled out; the booklet’s text and the set’s compilation are not claimed as public domain.

composer.born: 5 September 1867, Henniker, New Hampshire, United States
composer.died: 27 December 1944, New York City, United States
composer.epithet: American composer and former prodigy from New Hampshire who taught herself orchestration by attending Boston Symphony concerts; known for a symphony built on Irish tunes, first given in Boston.
facts: Piano with Ernst Perabo and Carl Baermann; one year of harmony with Junius Hill; otherwise self-taught

quote.text: I was not allowed to climb up on her lap, or on the music stool. I could only hear music, think music.
quote.source: Amy Beach on her mother’s rule, quoted in Sabrina Clarke, “Amy Beach the Synesthete”, WAM! Women and Music, Rutgers

composer.background:
Amy Marcy Cheney was born on 5 September 1867 in Henniker, New Hampshire, the only child of a paper manufacturer and a singer-pianist. At four she spent a summer on her grandfather’s farm in West Henniker, where there was no piano, and composed three waltzes in her head; she played them when she got home. Her mother would not teach her the piano until she was six. “I was not allowed to climb up on her lap, or on the music stool,” Beach remembered. “I could only hear music, think music.”

The Cheneys moved to Chelsea, Massachusetts, in 1871 and to Boston in 1875. Ernst Perabo and then Carl Baermann, a pupil of Liszt, taught her the piano; Junius Hill gave her a year of harmony. Boston musicians told her parents to send her to Europe. They kept her at home. On 24 October 1883, aged sixteen, she played Moscheles’s G minor Concerto and Chopin’s E♭ Rondo at the Boston Music Hall. Her first song in print, The Rainy Day, a Longfellow setting, appeared the same year. On 28 March 1885 she played Chopin’s F minor Concerto with the Boston Symphony under Wilhelm Gericke.
